utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic was born in Tuzla in 1971 and is of Bosnian Croat decent. Did his mandatory compulsory military service with the JNA military police from December 1990 until the end of March 1992. He then served for a short time in the ABiH, the Muslim army, at Mount Majevica and then went to the military police of the HVO, the Bosnian Croatian army, and served there from October 1992 until November 1993, when he left and went to the Republika Srpska. In April 1994, Mr. Erdemovic joined the VRS and became a member of the newly formed -- of a newly formed special unit which was renamed the 10th Sabotage Detachment in October 1994. Colonel Petar Salapura of the Main Staff was in charge of the unit, and the unit itself was commanded by 2nd Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis. A Major Pecanac also played a role in the unit, but Mr. Erdemovic was not aware of his position or exact role. In July 1995, the unit consisted of two platoons, about 30 members each, one located in Vlasenica, and the other in Bijeljina. Mr. Erdemovic was a member of the Bijeljina Platoon. On the afternoon of 10 July, Mr. Erdemovic, together with 30 to 40 other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, travelled from Bratunac, towards Srebrenica to take part in the attack on the enclave. They spent the night at an elevation above Srebrenica. On the morning of 11 July, Erdemovic and his unit descended into Srebrenica town. Their commander, Pelemis, told the members of the unit they would be joined by other units, including the Drina Wolves, and units from Bratunac and Milici. Pelemis told his unit to expect strong resistance when entering Srebrenica. Pelemis also told the unit, and I quote from Mr. Erdemovic's previous testimony: "That we were not to shoot at civilians in any case and that we were to direct them in front of us towards the stadium." From the Popovic testimony, 10944, lines 11 and 12. Mr. Erdemovic mentioned some of the members of his units present at Srebrenica on 11 July, including his commander, Milorad Pelemis; Bijeljina platoon commander, Franc Kos; and members Stanko Savanovic and Dragan Koljivrat; and Vlasenica platoon commander, Lule; and members Velimir Popovic and Zoran, nickname Maljic, and others. When Erdemovic and others reached the centre of Srebrenica town that afternoon near the mosque, an able bodied Muslim man surrendered to them. Pelemis ordered Zoran, nicknamed Maljic from the Vlasenica platoon, to kill this men. Erdemovic saw Zoran carry out this order by slitting the man's throat. Erdemovic and his units stayed in Srebrenica that night. The next day, on 12 July, they returned to Vlasenica where they had learned that Pelemis had overturned an armed personnel carrier near the Vlasenica base in Dragasevac. This killing, 10th Sabotage Detachment soldier, Dragan Koljivrat, from the Bijeljina platoon. On 13 July, Mr. Erdemovic and six to seven other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment travelled across Bosnia to Trebinje, near Dubrovnik, to attend Koljivrat's funeral. The journey to Trebinje took almost all day on the 13th. The funeral was held on the 14th and the group travelled back to Vlasenica during the night of the 14 July, arriving in Vlasenica on the morning of 15 July. On the morning of 16 July, Erdemovic and seven other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment commanded by Brano Gojkovic, departed from their base in Dragasevac for Zvornik. At the Zvornik brigade barracks, a tall, corpulent lieutenant-colonel with greyish hair in a VRS uniform came out of the barracks accompanied by two members of the Drina Corps military police. The lieutenant-colonel and the two MPs got into an olive-green-grey Opel Kadett car and led Erdemovic's group to a farm near the town of Pilica. The lieutenant-colonel went in side an office at the farm and then came out and spoke with Brano Gojkovic. At that time, Gojkovic announced that buses carrying civilians from Srebrenica would start arriving in a few minutes and they were to be killed. Soon thereafter, the lieutenant-colonel and two military policemen got back into the Opel Kadett, and as they were about to drive away from the area, the first busses with Muslim prisoners arrived. The first group of approximately ten prisoners was taken off a bus, blindfolded with their hands tied behind their backs. They were marched off some 100, 200 metres. Once the prisoners were in position, with their backs to their executioners, Brano Gojkovic gave the order to shoot. Mr. Erdemovic, along with the other seven members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, opened fire on the prisoners with automatic weapons. A second group of prisoners then followed, and Mr. Erdemovic and the other members of his unit executed them as well. The executions continued in this way from approximately 1000 hours until about 15 or 1600 hours with 15 to 20 bus loads of prisoners ultimately being executed. Mr. Erdemovic estimated that between 1.000 and 1200 people were executed at the farm that day. Early in the afternoon that day, eight to ten soldiers in VRS uniform arrived in a tam truck to the farm. Mr. Erdemovic believed that these men this come from Bratunac, because among other reasons, two members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment had recognised some of them as such. As the executions progressed, these soldiers kicked, punched, and cursed the prisoners. They also beat them with riffle butts and metal bars. Finally, the lieutenant-colonel came back to the farm as the last bus load of Muslims were being executed. The lieutenant-colonel told the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment unit that there were some 500 prisoners at the Pilica cultural centre who also needed to be executed. Mr. Erdemovic, as well as some other members of his squad, his colleagues, refused this order. Instead, members of the unit from Bratunac left the farm with the lieutenant-colonel. Mr. Erdemovic and the others were instructed to meet the lieutenant-colonel in a coffee bar in Pilica. When Erdemovic and others arrived at the coffee bar across the road from the Pilica cultural centre, he could see several dead bodies in front of the centre. Mr. Erdemovic heard gun-fire and explosions coming from the culture centre. At this time, Mr. Erdemovic saw vehicles passing by normally and people walking about. Mr. Erdemovic sat in the coffee bar with the lieutenant-colonel and two other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, Brano Gojkovic and Franc Kos. Later on, one of the soldiers from the unit of men from Bratunac came into the cafe and reported to the lieutenant-colonel that "everything had been finished." On January 14th, 1998, Mr. Erdemovic plead guilty to the charge of a violation of the laws or customs of war for his involvement in the participation in the summary execution of Muslim men from Srebrenica on 16 July 1995. Prior to his plea of guilty, Mr. Erdemovic and the Prosecution had entered into a Plea Agreement, wherein Mr. Erdemovic agreed to plead guilty to a violation of laws and customs of war and the Prosecution agreed to move to dismiss the alternative count of a violation of crimes against humanity. In the Plea Agreement, Mr. Erdemovic acknowledged the nature of the offence he was pleading guilty to, as well as the possible punishment he could face, including life imprisonment. He also acknowledged that he understood that the Trial Chamber was not bound by anything in the agreement between himself and the Prosecution and that sentencing was within the sole discretion of the Trial Chamber. Among other items set forth in the Plea Agreement, the Prosecution reported that Mr. Erdemovic had, up until then, provided considerable assistance to the Prosecution within the meaning of Rule 101(B)(ii) and agreed to address the Trial Chamber to a sentencing hearing and recommend seven years as the appropriate sentence. Mr. Erdemovic also agreed to continue to co-operate with the Prosecution and testify truthfully before the Tribunal if so requested by the Office of the Prosecutor. On 5 March 1998, the Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Erdemovic to five years imprisonment for the violation of the laws or customs of war. You see that in paragraph 23 of the Sentencing Judgement, dated 5 March 1998. Mr. Erdemovic has testified in the Rule 61 hearing against Karadzic and Mladic, back in, I believe, 1996, in the case OTP versus General Krstic, OTP versus Slobodan Milosevic, OTP versus Popovic et al, and, most recently, in OTP versus Perisic. His prior testimony was accepted in evidence in OTP versus Blagojevic and Jokic, pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, that's -- that's a lot. It's in the testimony, so I will just ask you some questions to clarify a few issues. Can you very briefly describe how it was, Mr. Erdemovic, that you -- well, you did your mandatory service in the JNA as described. We understand that. But how is it that you then became a member of, first, the BiH army, then the HVO, and then finally the VRS, throughout the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The -- I joined the BH army in 1992, because the conflict had erupted in Bosnia and all able-bodied men had to join the army. I did not stay there long. I was a scout on mortars and a few months later, in Tuzla, the Croatian Defence Council was established, and as I had a friend who was in the military police, I decided to join the military police so that I would avoid going to the front line. While I was with the military police at the HVO, I helped some Serb civilian who had remained in the Tuzla area and wanted to leave and cross over to the side that was under the control of the -- of the Republika Srpska army. I can't recall exactly what month it was. I believe in October or a little earlier. We were captured on Mount Majevica with few Serb civilians, so we were imprisoned and questioned about why we were helping Serb civilians and circumstances thereof. An individual whom I had helped before I was arrested, whom I had helped cross over into Republika Srpska, promised me that he would help me if I crossed over to the area which was under the control of the Republika Srpska army and that they would help me move abroad to Switzerland, namely; and that is why I decided to cross over to the territory that was under the control of the Republika Srpska army. However, that person did not keep his promise, so I had to remain in Republika Srpska and so I decided to join a unit in Bijeljina, which consisted of Croats, a Muslim, and a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At some point were you living in Serbia and had to leave around this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When I crossed over to Republika Srpska in the month of November, there were some individuals who recognised me who were from the Tuzla area, and they threatened me. So I decided to cross over to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at the time it was still the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But could I not stay there long because there, too, the military police and the civilian police arrested able-bodied individuals and sent them back to joined Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when did you first become a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have said in your previous statement that the 10th Sabotage was part of the Main Staff and that Colonel Salapura was in charge of it. Can you just briefly tell us how you knew that Colonel Salapura was in charge of the -- this Main Staff unit that you were part of, the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, in the beginning, the unit consisted of five to six Croat, a Muslim, and a Slovene, and it was a sabotage unit exclusively. Prior to an operation that was to be conducted in the Tuzla area, this person, from whom I later learned that he was Colonel -- this colonel and that he was Salapura, Petar Salapura. I learned that later on from the intelligence staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if he was in that role in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in early 1995, he came to the barracks -- or, rather, when this unit was in a -- in a small composition, they sent us to join a unit and because -- and as the unit grew, we were in the Bijeljina barracks so that, in 1995, early 1995, I saw this person again, Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say you saw him, is that it? You just saw him? Any idea of who he was, what he was there for, was there anything reliable about him, or did you just see him?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I knew that he was in charge of our unit. I knew this from before, when our unit was still small. I recall that day, because I was in charge of an operation, a mission in Tuzla. I was the commanding officer of that group, and I decided not to carry out that mission because I -- I felt, and I thought, that civilians might be endangered. And when we returned, because I was the commanding officer of this group, I was asked to explain why I did not allow this mission to go on and that is when I got to know Colonel Salapura even better and -- because he told me that I was lying, referring to what I had put down in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your rank at the time you were in charge of this mission to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I was a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And "vodnik," can that be interpreted as corporal sometimes, do you know, as you understand English now?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know you say this in your testimony, but because you have brought it up, can you give us a very brief description of what the sabotage unit's job was. What kind of work did you do? I don't need at this point specific missions, but just the kind of missions you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The type of missions we had was to try and move behind enemy lines unobserved, to collect data about enemy weapons and anything that related to the military. Blowing up and setting up explosives to sites where the enemy had their weapons, weapons depots, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've also mentioned in your testimony and some of your statements the name Pecanac. What do you know about him and his connections, if anything, in the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know much about him. He came occasionally. For instance, when we conducted reconnaissance missions in Srebrenica, he made an appearances, and then on our way back from Srebrenica, that -- on that night, on the 12th, when our commander had the accident in his vehicle, and Dragan Koljivrat was killed in the accident, he was there then. I didn't know much about him. I knew that he was a major, that he was called Pecanac. That's how people addressed him. And nothing else. He just came there from time to time and he did some work for our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've mentioned in your testimony, in statements, about a -- an operation that you went on through a tunnel to Srebrenica. And can you just briefly describe when you think that was and what that operation was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when this operation was carried out. I think it was in earlier 1995 or thereabout. It has to be in earlier 1995. We entered through a tunnel, an underground tunnel, that connected a place near Bratunac and came out at the other end, in Srebrenica. That mission was supposed to alert the military and the population, the people in Srebrenica, it was a sort of reconnaissance sortee. [In English] Sorry, I can't find the word in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did -- what did the unit do once it went through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We came into Srebrenica at midnight. We fired a few flares or a few missiles, rockets. We had small-arms, and this lasted all in all about ten minutes, and then we returned via the same way under the -- through the tunnel, to the area which was under the control of VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you co-ordinate or connect with any members of the Bratunac Brigade, before, during, or after this mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were two men there - I don't know if they were from the Bratunac Brigade, I think so - who knew about the tunnel. And I think that one of the people who actually led us through the tunnel had worked at the mine, so he knew exactly which tunnel would come out at the Srebrenica end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said that rockets were fired. Can you describe to us what kind of weapon this was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: These were former JNA Zoljas. [In English] I'm struggling for words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A Zolja, is that, like, what in English we would call rocket-propelled grenades, a shoulder-fired grenade weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these Zoljas were fired from the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've estimated that that day at Branjevo farm the group killed between 1000 and 1200 people. How did you get that estimate?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived at the figure - and I don't know if it is correct - but by counting the buses. I didn't actually count them, but I assessed it was -- it stayed with me that it could have been about that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And going now to Pilica village as you were at this cafe. Can you describe what if anything was going on in the town while this -- while you were across the street from the Pilica cultural centre, both the normal and abnormal.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Between the cultural centre and the cafe there was a civilian check-point manned by the civilian police, Republika Srpska civilian police, vehicles drove through normally. But not far from there, one could hear shots and shells being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there any people or vehicles on the street that you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian vehicles went through those check-points. Everything seemed normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you conclude was going on at the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Before they left the farm, this colonel came and he said there were 500 people in the Pilica culture hall and that they should also be shot, and I and some people from my unit refused that and we stayed behind. But the persons who were -- were talking, some people from my unit, from Bratunac, they already left. We hadn't even left the farm when you could hear the shots and the hand-grenades exploding. We could hear that. They were coming from the direction of the Pilica Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall your unit receiving any training in the FRY -- what would have been the FRY prior to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe, you know, when that was and the kind of training you got. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think this was in late 1994 or early 1995. Perhaps it was in December 1994. I cannot remember. The training was actually such that they went to the army barracks in Pancevo. This was the Army of Yugoslavia, and that's where they had the training, to learn how to use different kinds of weapons, to place explosives, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go do that training in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document. It's number 2074. This is a document I showed you on Sunday, and both versions should come up. I hope you can read one of them. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is now an exhibit, as I suppose, you could perhaps indicate which P number we have for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- this is not one of the ones I mentioned to you because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, my mistake. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could blow up the -- the Serbo-Croatian one, the one that we see now. I think for much of our purposes that language helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that this is dated the 10th of July, 1995. It's from the Command of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. It's an order that Franc Kos, leader group -- is -- are any of those men familiar, those names that are listed in this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Franc Kos, Marko Boskic, Brano Gojkovic. My name is there. Dragan Koljivrat, Zoran, Stanko Sovanovic, Stipan, Zoran -- Stupar, Zoran; Lulis [phoen], Goran; Vlastimir Golijan. These are all the people from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we drop down in the English a bit so we can see who signs off in on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we -- we see that this has been signed by Franc Kos for Milorad Pelemis. Have you ever -- did you see this -- this order back then, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It doesn't say precisely what you're to do. But given the date of this, 10 July, and the route that it takes, does this order have anything to do with the operation that you were involved in, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that next to your name it says, "Sergeant." And you have, over the years, and in your statements and testimonies, talked about your authority. Were you a sergeant at the time, as this notes?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time, actually, before then, like I said, I already had a conflict with 2nd Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis, and I also had a conflict with Colonel Salapura, because they -- because I didn't want to do what they wanted me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned a few minutes ago that I refused to carry out an order by Salapura, because I was at this location where the assignment was to have been carried out. And I decided that the civilian population would have been endangered and harmed and that is why, as I said already, wrote a report and they said that these were lies, and so on. Also, at a -- during an action before where I was the commander of that group, I decided to release one person that we had captured at the Majevica mountain. That person was here to testify about how I had decided to release them, and that is why Pelemis always objected to that. He -- he -- he always held that against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you recall we showed you that document yesterday, and Mr. Janc, the investigator whom you met, made a brief note that said after showing that document to you that: "Erdemovic confirmed that he was a sergeant at the time of the group and, at the time, but that -- having a group leader. But having had a dispute with Petar Salapura, he was not a leader anymore." So just to clarify, is -- were you -- is this document correct: Were you a sergeant at the time like indicates in this proofing note?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Like I already said, at that point in time, I was just a regular soldier. Pelemis told me that I was not going to be the group leader anymore and that I would have a rank no longer. This was much before the Srebrenica events unfolded. This was in early 1995. So to my mind, I know that he told me that, and I know that I wasn't a sergeant or a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the fall of 1995, do you remember that there was some kind of awards ceremony at Dragasevac, the Vlasenica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in Dragasevac. That was when -- this was in late 1995. I was, again, given the rank of corporal or Sergeant, and -- I don't know how to explain this. I was like a first class sabotage officer, seconds class sabotage officer, depending on how many actions you had taken part in, and then would you given this kind of title, sabotage officer, first class sabotage officer, second class; I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would like to offer 2074 into evidence. I had forgotten to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Erdemovic, have you seen over the years, and actually yesterday as well in my office, a portions of a video of that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you be seen, yourself, at some point in the -- during the festivities?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a short and edited clip of -- of the video that we have of a more complete version, but we have a short clip I'd like to show the witness and just ask him to identify himself and perhaps another person or two. And it's 1378.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read the Cyrillic date on that? I don't know how well you are with Cyrillic, but ... I don't think we have to worry about the date. I see it now, so don't worry about it. Let's just continue to play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it will be not be broadcast out of this courtroom, because if the -- the witness is shown on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first parts of it are fine, and Ms. Stewart will tell me, and I think -- I hope that way will work. There is this last segment that we can keep from the public. But I think we can catch it. So the first part is fine publicly, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person in the middle is General Krstic. To his right is commander of our unit, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who's the person with the moustache that is reading something?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That was in our -- that person was in our unit. He was in charge of paperwork and reading out orders. His name is Savo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this still can be seen at 20.3 on the counter, for the record. If we can continue to play, and I'll stop it if I need to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is that you that they referred to getting some kind of a promotion?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was in late 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. We saw -- yeah, in a kind of subtitle, this is, I think, a translation of what is said, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. This is the -- it's being played in a software called Sanction, and it's a particular kind of subtitling of the transcript that will go in with the video as part of the record. And I should note that the reference that he just made about his name and sergeant was at 57.2 in that -- on that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this part should not be broadcast, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're not quite there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard the name of this witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: His name is fine, Mr. President, being public. It's -- it is kinds of a strange situation, a unique situation, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, we can continue to play it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is at 1.12.7 on the counter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, General Krstic. The person in the middle is Milorad Pelemis. He is pointing to the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We're at 2.13.4, and right before that we saw General Krstic. And now this person in the middle is Pelemis, is that right, that's pointing down on the table?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the commander of our unit, Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's 2.22.9. And up until now, have you recognised anybody else besides the people that you have pointed out as you've watched it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a different scene of -- of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who are these guys and what is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is what can't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am there on this image. I'm the third person from the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I probably confused the issue. Can you tell us what this is, this -- with everybody sitting at the table. Who are these people, and does it have anything to do with the formal ceremony we just saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened afterwards, in the Vlasenica cultural hall, after this ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who are the people around you? I don't need names. Just generally who are all these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: These are people from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's just play it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I read in the summary, you have told -- always reported that upon entering the centre of Srebrenica near a mosque, Pelemis ordered the murder of a Muslim, a military-aged man, that came up to your group. And I showed you some video yesterday. I want to show you -- for the first time, I want to show you some video now and ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this can be broadcast, and it's 5497.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the person that Pelemis ordered, Zoran Maljic, to kill, this is somebody living in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue to play the video and see if there's anything that you may recognise in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I can conclude, this is the centre of Srebrenica town. I'd never been to Srebrenica before then. So this is the mosque, and that would be the person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just finish up this segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would like to offer the exhibit of the ceremony, which is 1378, into evidence, and that one segment where he identified himself should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering them as separate exhibits? One public, one under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it would be best if we could get two clips, the public and the private, and that way we stay more private. And Ms. Stewart will help us so we can get it right. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both portions of this video will be received as separate exhibits. The second one, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The public version of 65 ter 1378 will be Exhibit P234. The -- the second version of 1378 will be Exhibit P235, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would offer this short clip of the centre of town as 5497 into evidence, and I'll -- there is more video related to that that will come in later. But I think since he has spoke of this section, we should get this section in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is appreciated to identify correctly which portion we have seen. This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P236.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is a convenient time for a break. And after the break, you may cross-examine the witness, Mr. Tolimir. We must have our first break now on technical reasons, and the Court Officer will assist you during the break. We will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We had left that we have a full Bench now this afternoon. Now we will continue the hearing with the cross-examination by Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And again I would wish a good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, and may God's peace reign in this house, and I wish that this trial proceedings end with God's help and not according to my wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address the witness now and please have understanding from my asking questions to you that may sometimes related to issues that have you already testified about in other cases, and I hope it won't be too difficult to answer those questions for the transcript of these proceedings. Thank you. And also would you please make a pause and answer my question only after I say "thank you" at the end of my question to enable the interpreters to do their jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to remind you that during the answer of the witness, you should switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can use the other microphone. Otherwise, we will have this, yeah, disturbance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will switch on the other microphone. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 10928, lines 20 through 24, you confirmed, that on the 5th of March of 1988 [as interpreted] you were sentenced to five years imprisonment and that you have served your sentence. Could you now please tell us for the transcript how many years you were -- how many years you served in prison, including the years when you were in remand at the Tribunal's detention unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998 you were sentenced to five years imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall exactly how many years I was imprisoned. I think over three years. I was sentenced to five years, but because I served my prison term in Norway, under the Norwegian laws, I was released after a certain period elapsed. I can't recall exactly how much sooner that was. But I think that I served some three-plus years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here that you were a member of the JNA, and then a member of the BH army, and then in the HVO, and then, finally, in the VRS. Could you please tell us for the transcript whether all of this happened between 1991 and 1995 and if you can, please tell us what army you served in what periods. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you said, in 1991, I was in the regular JNA army and my service there ended, if I remember correctly, in March 1992. I don't know exactly when I joined the BH army, but I didn't stay there long. This was in the course of 1992, in any case. And three months later because I think I was in the BH army for three months, three months later, I joined the military police of the Croatian defence council was established in Tuzla. In 1993, I crossed over to the territory under the control of the VRS but I did not join the VRS immediately, it only happens some five months later or so, sometime in April 1994. So I joined the VRS in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what units you serve in the JNA and where were you deployed. We need this in order to understand why you were assigned to a Sabotage Unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the JNA, I served in Slavonia. I was deployed in Slavonia. First I was in Belgrade with the military police, and then I was transferred to the Slavonia, to the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us for the transcript, please, how long you served in the military police and also how long you served in the units that saw some fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 through 1992, March. I believe March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, were you assigned to these police units where you served in the BH army and the HVO because you had some experience in police units, and you had undergone military training and you also had some combat experience notice war itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, in the BH army, I was a scout, a mortar unit scout, and I decided to joined military police, the HVO military police, because the duties of the military police, within the HVO, included providing security for the command, the garrison, and I did not have to be assigned to the front line as other soldiers did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In Vukovar, were you in infantry or guards units or military police units? And were you assigned to military police jobs and assignments or combat.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for a while, we provided security or guards duty for the command, and after that, we were assigned to the front line as soldiers on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you complete your military service before or after the Vukovar fighting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "as a soldier"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was told that it is better that you have the microphone directly to your head and not to the side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for wasting the Court's time and having to repeat this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But please just tell us briefly, did you complete your military service in Vukovar and did this happen after the operations in Slavonia ended? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I completed my full year of service, which was the regular term, and then because the state of war was declared, we were extended by three months. Each of us had to stay for three extra months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said already that you reported when received call-up papers from the BH army that you went to the Territorial Defence and that you joined the army then. Can you just confirm this? Is that what you did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1029, pages 20 through 24 in the Popovic transcript, you confirmed that on the 5th of March, 1998, you were sentenced to five years in prison and that you served your prison sentence. Could you tell us, for the transcript, please, whether your Plea Agreement had any impact on the length of your service and on the terms that you served, and did you serve the full term? And could you tell us how all of that happened? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how to answer your question, but I will do my best. The Plea Agreement meant the following: The Prosecution proposed a seven-year sentence, but it was also -- the possibility was also open that I would be sentenced to a life sentence, and it was really up to the Trial Chamber to make that decision as to what my prison term would be. At least that was what I was explained and what was told to me by my Defence counsel, Mr. Jovan Babic. That's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We understood. The Defence council had a role to play there, that is undisputed. Now tell us, please, said that you were taken prisoner while you were in the HVO. You didn't tell us who you were taken prisoner by. The BH army or the VRS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken prisoner by the HVO because I helped Serb population move from the area of Tuzla to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just tell us why the Serb population was leaving Tuzla for Bijeljina, which was in Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I explain this to you? I think that they wanted to cross over to the area that was in Republika Srpska because they were people of Serb ethnicity and perhaps they felt safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of any instances where these people felt unsafe or whether they were harassed or in some other way mistreated, why they would want to leave there and leave everything behind for a place where they had nothing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that some people were arrested in Tuzla because they were of Serb ethnicity. I didn't really know why people were being arrested or not. I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the Trial Chamber and I will have a better understanding of what you are telling us if you tell us how it was that you organised this transfer of the population from the BH army to the territory which was under the control of the VRS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility -- the HVO area of responsibility, which was on Mount Majevica, was an area which I was very well familiar with. I knew where the trenches were and everything else. And as for the Serb population that I helped move over to Bijeljina, most ever these people were people whom I knew who were from my circles. They were my neighbours from the Donje Travinje [phoen], and I didn't really know people who were from other areas in Tuzla. I helped those people who were my neighbours, as it were, whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will I correct in saying that, in fact, the HVO unit was actually a buffer zone between the BH army territory and the VRS territory and that you actually transferred and helped people cross over from one area to the other through their territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I put this? The unit, or the area that was under the Croatian Defence Council was actually a unit from the BH army on Mount Majevica, but they were under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, I think because most of the villages in that area were Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us this: Did this unit of yours, the HVO unit, was it on the border-line with -- did it have a direct border with the -- with the Republika Srpska and was the line -- the demarkation line, as it were, there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is clear. Now, could you tell us, please, whether you were in any way rewarded for transferring these people from one territory to the other, did you get any kind of remuneration?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well the reward that I got, and we're talking about 20 to 30 people, the -- in order to get to the area, we had to go through several check-points, and there was a shortage of fuel in Tuzla at the time, so I got the fuel from them. That was the only reward that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So there was no reward, no remuneration, no profits, just the cost of the fuel; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please - I will now move onto another area - when you left for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and you said in the Popovic transcript that, in 1994, on page 10933, lines --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the line numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say the following and yet there, in early 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... they began mobilisation, so that I was unable to return to Republika Srpska." Is this what you said and have I quoted your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please clarify something here, both for me and for the Trial Chamber and perhaps for your own sake, why would you, as a Croat, be mobilised in Belgrade, and then deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina where would you fight for the Serbian army? Did you have some other documents or -- with you or -- could you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not in Belgrade. I was in Titov Vrbas staying with a friend, and the only documents that I had on me was my old ID, the IDs that we all had while Yugoslavia was still one country. There was, on the ID, the name of my father and the place and date of my birth. There was nothing else on that ID. There was no indication as to my ethnicity, whether I was Croatian or Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've made that clear. So, in other words, you were sent based on your ID and then when you realised that would you have to join the fighting, you decided to return to the unit where you were before; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this question about the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you a member of some unit of the Army of Republika Srpska before 1994? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you been in Serbia before that, and then, when under threat that you would be mobilised, did you go then back to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As for the Sabotage Detachment, did you report into it because it was of mixed composition, it had several Croats and Muslims; or were you assigned to go to that because that was the place you would be assigned on the basis of military archives or your military speciality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to Republika Srpska and I went, once again, to my wife, who was Serbian. She had some relatives there in Bijeljina, so we went to the military department in Bijeljina, and that was when I learned that it would be the best for me to join that unit. And that was what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went to the unit voluntarily. You were not forced to join it nor were you assigned to it because of your earlier deserts [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I joined it of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor mentioned here, and so did you, that an agreement was signed between you and the Prosecution. My question is whether you were promised anything on that occasion in terms of the change of your place of residence, the length of your sentence, the change of your identity, and so on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, the OTP proposed a length of sentence of seven years. However, the length of sentence did not depend on me or on the Prosecutor. The Court was to decide how many years I would be sentenced to. As for the next question, that is to say, my transfer to another country, the Prosecutor never discussed that with me. It was afterwards when I had already been sentenced and when I was in Norway, it was decided that, because of my name and because of everything that happened, it would be good if I changed that, and if the country in which I would spend my later life would not be public [as interpreted]. As far as I remember, I never discussed that with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So the length of sentence was determined by the Trial Chamber rather than by the OTP. Did I understand that properly or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the OTP proposed seven years whereas I was sentenced to five years. It means to me that the Judges were the ones who decided about the length of sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us now why did you sign an agreement saying that you would confess your guilt and you agreed to testify in all cases to which the OTP invited you to testify, and you testified in almost all the cases. Did that affected the length of sentence in any way or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Even before this agreement, I stated when I testified in my own case, and when I was to declare whether I was guilty or not, I agreed to testify in other cases. In these cases, your name and names of others were not mentioned. Only the names of Karadzic and Mladic were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the explanation. So it was not a part of the obligation when you reached an agreement with the OTP that you should testify in -- in other cases, in my case now, or in the Karadzic case or eventually possibly in the Mladic case or whoever would appear before this Court. Is that so or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, I said even before we reached an agreement that I would testify in other cases. Your name, of course, was not mentioned, and many names of persons in whose cases I testified were not mentioned. But in this agreement, I obliged myself to testify in all cases in which I was invited to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I think I have understood you. Did you have any personal problems or personal motives in connection any other people? Because you said here that you were in a conflict with some of your superiors. Or was it only in -- because the Prosecution asked you about some specific persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: To be frank, in case of Milorad Pelemis, I said immediately that I wished to testify against him and also Salapura. As for you and some other persons against whom I did testify, I have no reasons whatsoever. Let me explain. First of all, I have never seen you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have understood what you said. We have heard that did you have certain problems with Pelemis and Gojkovic and there were even problems when you had to carry out the orders, that was why you were replaced or stripped of your rank, as you said here. Did I quote that correctly from the previous transcripts, or should I refer to the transcripts? You even said that in the statements which you gave in Yugoslavia; for example, in Novi Sad and whatever. I would not like to waste time and pull up these statements. But did I quote your words correctly or not? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just explain. I know for certain that Pelemis sent me to that farm on that particular day. Therefore, I still feel within me, this, I don't like this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have understood. You had personal problems and personal conflicts. Was it also based on the material conditions of your life in Bijeljina or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the last question. You have asked me several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm sorry. As soon as the interpreters interpret this, I will ask you a clear question. Did your conflict with your superior result from a personal conflict with them; or was it also caused by your material situation in which you were living in Bijeljina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: My disagreements with Pelemis, as far as I could see this person, he was not interested in anyone. He didn't care for anyone, he didn't favour anyone. I think that he just wanted to achieve what he wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For example, in Novi Sad, you told the district court in Novi Sad the following. I can refer to the document. It's 1D133.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could show it on the screen but there is nothing contentious about the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read it to you: "In early February, 1995, I signed agreement as a professional soldier and I started to undergo training. And I was assigned commander of the 1st Sabotage Detachment." My question is: When you were assigned and given a rank, and you became the commander of Sabotage Detachment in February 1995, did you get more points for your salary. So was that one of the reasons why you were not properly treated by others or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question so that it would be clearer. In the second part you say that they stripped you of your rank. Now the question is: Were they allowed to strip you of your rank? Only the person who awarded you the rank could strip you of the rank. They probably didn't award you the rank. So when they stripped you of your rank, did they also take away the income which you earned in the army and which helped you to sustain yourself and your family? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is basing his question on a quote from a document, I think -- if we could allow the witness, especially because it is on the screen, it is probably on the witness's screen, could he see the section that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you give, perhaps, a clearer reference, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is 1D133. I made the reference, but I said that I could just quote this to the witness so that he could read it too. And as for the stripping him of his rank, it is the transcript from the Popovic case, page 10963. So if the witness has a need to read it, or the Trial Chamber, then you might read both documents. For the sake of being economical and saving time, I wanted just to read it out to the witness because this question was not so important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an important statement. All questions are important. This is not on the accused's list of exhibits, yet it's the first thing he brings up. I would appreciate a complete list. If I don't have it, I would like us to get one, please. But, again, if he is quoting the -- the -- a portion of this, I think I would request the Court that the witness be allowed to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate that as well. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. As far as I know, the list has been submitted to the Registry and to the Trial Chamber and to the OTP. We submitted the first list several days ago. And this morning, we just added two or three documents, two of which are already in e-court as these are Prosecution documents. But we just pulled out several pages. This is why we did today. Otherwise everything has been submitted, and everything functions perfectly on our computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Gajic. We have received the Defence list of potential exhibits for this witness, and there is mentioning of 1D133. And if I'm not mistaken, we have that on the screen before us. But perhaps you need another page of this document. And if there's an English translation, we would appreciate to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told there was no English translation. Are you referring to the first page of this document, Mr. Tolimir, or another page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I meant to refer to page 4 in B/C/S, but it is not so important because the witness and I have understood each other. But for your reference, it's page 4 in B/C/S, just so you can see that I quoted correctly from the document, and as the Prosecutor said it was important for him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a long text on page 4. Which part are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have a look at the line which begins with numbers 60 to 70 in B/C/S. First it says: "60 to 70 men and then the 1st of February, 1995, I signed a professional military agreement." And then: "We began our training but I got the rank of sergeant and I was assigned commander of the 1st Sabotage Group. I signed this agreement with the Serbian army." I have quoted this and the witness has understood what I said. It is page 4, 23rd -- line 23, from the top of the page in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you -- you saw it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is the reason why I wanted him to see it. The question sounded like he was the commander of the entire Sabotage Unit, and now it is clear that he was in command of a small group. And if I could ask when these statements are given if they could send it to our Case Manager. I don't always see every e-mail an hour or two before I come to court, which apparently I was on the list, but Ms. Stewart wasn't and that would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Erdemovic, do you want to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did sign a contract with the Army of Republika Srpska. I was a sergeant. I was awarded the rank of Sergeant. At the time I was the commander of one group in the Bijeljina Platoon, but after that, I also said in the same text that conflicts arose between Pelemis and myself. I said that earlier when I was questioned by the Prosecution that conflicts arose because they told me that I was lying to them when I said that certain actions could not be carried out, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erdemovic. You have seen that I quoted your words literally. Now I will quote what you said in further text. It's on page 10933 from the Popovic case. You said in lines 8 to 12. In answer to the Prosecutor's question you say, when he asked you: "What was your rank and position at the time in the unit?" And you say, on lines 8 through 12: "Before that, I was a lance corporal in the VRS army in the 10th Sabotage Unit, but because I had a clash with Pelemis who was the unit commander, he stripped me of my rank and I was, in fact, a commander of a group in the Bijeljina Platoon but I was a mere private." Have I quoted your words correctly and is this what you stated in the Popovic case, in answer to the Prosecutor's question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: If I said that, that I was a lance corporal, that's an error, and I apologise. I was a sergeant, and the contract between me and the VRS was shown here in The Hague, and everything is stated clearly there, when it was that I became a sergeant, and all the other details. I don't know where that contract is, but I had occasion to see it here before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly as you said. That's in Prosecutor 65 ter 01378. And it states there that you were a reserve infantry sergeant and not a mere private; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Where is it stated? Can you please clarify what document you're referring to? I don't have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution document, 65 ter number 03 -- 01378.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document was shown, actually, it's a video-clip - we've seen it today - on the occasion of the celebration of the 10th Sabotage Unit. This is shown on minutes 4.38 through 4.48 of that video-clip. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could see that on the video-clip. That was toward the end of 1995, but I can't recall exactly what month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So am I right in saying that you could not be stripped of the rank of sergeant because here it says that you were a sergeant. Am I correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I've explained before, I know that I did sign the contract which states that I am a sergeant. I believe this was in February; I'm not sure of the exact date. But if you say so, that's probably correct. But because of the conflict that I had with Pelemis, and anyone can confirm this, any member of my unit, Pelemis said to me that I was no longer a group commander, that from then onwards, I was to be a mere private, and I believe this was in April 1995, which is when I was stripped of the rank and demoted and became a private, and I did not command any other unit. The ceremony, the celebration that we saw at the end of 1995, at this ceremony it was decided again that I was reinstated as a sergeant. Why? I really can't explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just answer this: Did you stop receiving a salary, according to the contract where you were appointed as a sergeant. Can you just tell us that? Did you stop receiving that salary. That's all I want to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: If I can remember this correctly, but this was 15 or 16 years ago, but as far as I can recall, all privates and I, as a sergeant, we all had the same pay. I believe that the platoon -- from the platoon commander and higher, the pay was somewhat higher. But I can't really say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me this: When it was proclaimed again that you were -- when you were reinstated as a sergeant, did you accept that or did Pelemis strip you of that rank again? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: At this time I had just returned from Belgrade after surgery, after I was wounded. I think this was in October, sometime in October. I was told that I had to go to Vlasenica for the units celebration, and I had no idea that this was going to be read out about me. I knew that if you spent a certain time in a certain unit, depending on how many missions you participated in, you would be assigned a class. So I was then -- I was then said -- I was then promoted to sabotage officer, first class or second class.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us who was it who could propose you for promotion or for a rank? Would that have to be someone from your unit or someone from a superior units to yours? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a squad leader within that platoon, did you propose anyone for promotion, or did your sergeant propose people for propose? Do you recall? Who would it be who would actually propose someone for promotion, if you can recall? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I knew it would all depend on how a mission was accomplished, and also on the number of missions you participated in, whether they were successful and what your conduct was in the mission, whether you had accomplished it or not and stuff like that. How would I -- how would I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tolimir, I had to stop your next question because the translation was not finished yet. Now proceed, please, and pause between -- after the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, in order to complete this picture relating to ranks and so on, could you please tell us, were you a private or not, or, rather, were you a sergeant or not, as we could see in that video-clip or not, although it is not really relevant?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're absolutely right. It was really of no relevance to me whether I was a sergeant or not. But if that's what it said there in the video-clip, then I was a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erdemovic. We will now move on to another group of issues. And again this has to do with your relationship with certain individuals. Now I would like do talk about Brano Gojkovic. You mentioned that person in your statement and also during your evidence in the Popovic case where you said that you were not on good terms with him. Am I correct or not in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't on good terms but I wasn't -- I didn't have a bad relationship with Brano Gojkovic either. I did not -- I was not in the same platoon. I was in Vlasenica, he was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I was in Bijeljina, he was in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we didn't really see each other very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he of a higher rank than you were or not? Could you please tell me?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I think he was a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the military chain of command he was mere private, whereas you were a non-commissioned officer. Thank you. Could you now just tell us one more thing: Who was Mr. Kremenovic, and what can you tell us about this person, Kremenovic, and what his role was in your unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Radoslav Kremenovic was a lieutenant. He was deputy commander of our unit, and as you could see there, Lieutenant-Colonel [as interpreted] Milorad Pelemis was the commander and the lieutenant was his deputy. So these individuals who had ranks in our unit, they could actually command to a person of higher rank and this person, as I've already said was the deputy in our unit and that person was a very pleasant, easy going individual you could talk to and explain your problems, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, line 22, says -- sorry now I've lost it, but it referred to Pelemis as a lieutenant-colonel. That should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, which page and which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps it got fixed. It said Pelemis was a lieutenant-colonel and I just wanted it corrected. I don't see that anymore. So maybe it got fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You raised too early. Not patient enough. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Erdemovic. You have just explained this perfectly because this Kremenovic was a lieutenant, and Pelemis was the second lieutenant; so here we had a situation where a second lieutenant was a commander to a lieutenant, correct? Is that what situation was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, whether Kremenovic was arrested at the same time when you were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did he have any role in your transfer to The Hague and did he come with you to The Hague voluntarily and then was released and sent back; or was he -- did he come to The Hague as an accused? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it was that Kremenovic came The Hague and under what conditions, whether he was an accused or a witness, I can't really describe. But after Kremenovic and I were arrested in his house, I can't remember in what town it was in Serbia, from that moment on I had no further contacts with Kremenovic. And my Defence counsel had no information about him of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It was mentioned that he, too, was brought to The Hague. Was that the case? Thank you. It was said in the public that he, too, was brought to The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was true. Kremenovic, too, came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he in charge of your platoon and was he in Srebrenica with you, or was someone else the platoon commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I already described, he was a deputy commander of our unit. He was not in Srebrenica. They were on some other mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, who was in charge of your unit there Srebrenica then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Franc Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have a rank at the time or was he a private? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was the second lieutenant. I think he was given this rank of second lieutenant, but I can't really be quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Brano Gojkovic of a higher rank compared to him or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is that in your statement you say at one point that Gojkovic issued orders. Does that mean that he issued orders to Kos as well although he didn't have a rank higher than his? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, that is suggesting that this occurred at Srebrenica, and he has mixed up the two incidents at the farm and Srebrenica. If he could be clear so that the witness understands what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I asked the witness whether Kos or Gojkovic, rather, was Kos's superior when they were at the farm or not, because the witness said that he had issued orders there to Kos although Kos had a higher rank. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that happened at the Branjevo farm, Brano and Aleksander Cvetkovic they were the organisers of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's clarify one more thing. We have 1D132. Could we please see that. This is from the Popovic case when Mr. Todorovic testified, who will also appear in this case. In the transcript on page 14041, lines 16 through 24, I quote the OTP witness, Todorovic: "I know that Mr. Gojkovic did not have orders, that did he not have a rank, that he could not issue commands, that he should not command any member of the Sabotage Unit." And then he says again in the question. I quote: "Well, do you know who was in the group that went to the farm then? He says: "It was Franc Kos who was a second lieutenant, and had he not been there, this would have been done by Drazen Erdemovic who would signed that document." And now, in view of this, my question is the following: Did I quote this correctly and could you read this in the transcript, seeing that you know English and speak English?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand what equipment you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, these are Todorovic's words. I just quoted what he said. He was saying about this Gojkovic person, that he had issued equipment to soldiers and not to issue orders. And you said: "I know that did he not have" -- he said, "I know that he did not have a rank, that he could not issue orders to any members of the sabotage group." And then you say: "All right. Well, do you know who was in charge of that group who had left?" And you said Franc Kos, who was the sergeant, and who signed off on the equipment, and if he hadn't been there, then that paper would have been signed by Drazen Erdemovic. Is this what you said? I just want you to confirm because I don't want the Trial Chamber to think that you said things that weren't -- that I said things that weren't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have many problems. The first is I didn't understand who was testifying in this transcript. The second is if you read something out, you should slow down. It is very complicated for the record and for the interpreters. Could you please again indicate who is testifying in this transcript we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked that page 1 -- or actually 1D132 be pulled up on the monitors. This is the testimony of Dragan Todorovic who will appear as a witness in this trial as well. And he mentioned all three individuals here and their hierarchy, and I mentioned the relevant portions of his transcript -- of his testimony in the case, on page 14041 in the transcript, line 16 through 24, and I said what he said. That he knew that Gojkovic could not issue any orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
